Thanks for picking this up — I hit the same crash and can confirm the root-cause analysis is spot on. But I tested this PR's shim on Windows and **it still fails**, just with a different error than the original. Sharing a full repro so we can get a version that actually lands.

**Environment:** Windows 11 (10.0.26200), Bun 1.3.13, Node v24.14.0, gbrain on `master` (postinstall still uses the POSIX one-liner — unfixed as of today).

### The `node -e` shim doesn't parse under Bun's Windows script-runner

Running this PR's exact `postinstall` via `bun install` / `bun run postinstall` on Windows:

```
$ node -e "const{spawnSync}=require('child_process');...process.stderr.write('[gbrain] postinstall skipped. See https://github.com/garrytan/gbrain/issues/218
')}"
[eval]:1
...issues/218
                  ^^^^
SyntaxError: Invalid or unexpected token
    at makeContextifyScript (node:internal/vm:194:14)
```

The `\n` at the end of the hint string is the problem. Bun's built-in script-runner (which runs lifecycle scripts on Windows — there's no `/bin/sh`) **expands `\n` into a real newline before `node` ever sees the string**. That newline lands inside the single-quoted JS string literal, so `node -e` throws `SyntaxError: Invalid or unexpected token`. Minimal repro, no gbrain involved:

```
# package.json -> "postinstall": "node -e \"process.stderr.write('hi\n')\""
$ bun run postinstall
[eval]:1
process.stderr.write('hi
SyntaxError: Invalid or unexpected token
```

So this is the **same bug class** as the original report — *the lifecycle shell mangles the script string before the interpreter runs it* — just relocated from POSIX redirect grammar to a JS string-literal escape. It likely passed locally because the shell you tested on preserves `\n` as the two characters `\` + `n` (which `node` then reads as a newline escape); Bun's Windows runner expands it instead. It's shell-dependent.

### Two smaller notes on the approach

1. **`node` isn't guaranteed under a Bun install.** The PR body says "bun is built on top of node on every platform" — Bun is actually a from-scratch runtime (Zig + JavaScriptCore) and doesn't require Node. A Bun-only user may not have `node` on PATH. Since this is a `bun install` lifecycle hook, **`bun` is the guaranteed-present runtime, not `node`.** (In practice many machines have both — mine does — so this is a portability nit, not the blocker. The newline above is the blocker.)
2. **`shell: process.platform === 'win32'` re-introduces a shell on Windows**, so `gbrain apply-migrations` gets launched through `cmd.exe` — re-opening a (smaller) quoting surface. Resolving the binary and spawning with an argv array and no shell avoids that.

### Suggestion: move the logic into a file

Both the original and this shim fail because they **embed a program inside a package.json string**, where the lifecycle shell can mangle it. The robust fix is to not put the program in the string at all — keep package.json to `bun run scripts/postinstall.ts` (the pattern the repo already uses for ~19 other scripts) and put the logic in a real file:

```ts
// scripts/postinstall.ts
import { which } from 'bun';
const HINT =
  '[gbrain] postinstall skipped. If installed via `bun install -g github:...`: ' +
  'run `gbrain doctor` and `gbrain apply-migrations --yes` manually. ' +
  'See https://github.com/garrytan/gbrain/issues/218';
const bin = which('gbrain');                 // Windows-aware PATH resolve (finds gbrain.exe)
if (!bin) { console.error(HINT); process.exit(0); }
try {
  const r = Bun.spawnSync([bin, 'apply-migrations', '--yes', '--non-interactive'],
    { stdout: 'inherit', stderr: 'inherit' });  // argv array, no shell
  if (r.exitCode !== 0) console.error(HINT);
} catch { console.error(HINT); }
process.exit(0);                              // never abort the install
```

```diff
-    "postinstall": "command -v gbrain >/dev/null 2>&1 && ... 1>&2",
+    "postinstall": "bun run scripts/postinstall.ts",
```

`bun` is guaranteed present in a Bun lifecycle script, `Bun.which` resolves `gbrain.exe` (the old `command -v` couldn't), the argv array means no shell grammar to mangle, and it keeps the exact #218 hint + the never-fail-the-install contract. **Verified on the environment above:** `bun install` completes, migrations run ("All migrations up to date."), exit 0; and with `gbrain` absent from PATH it prints the hint and still exits 0.

Confirming this independently — and flagging that it's **still unfixed on latest `master` (v0.42.12.0)**, ~6 weeks and dozens of releases after this was filed against 0.14.2.

**My setup:** source / `bun link` install, pinned at 0.42.1.0, local HEAD 19 commits behind `origin/master`. A daily `gbrain check-update --json` cron has been silently returning `error: "no_releases"` / `update_available: false` on every run — i.e. exactly this blind spot, in production. Nothing locally modified in the update path.

**The root cause is simpler than "source-install-specific" — the release source is empty for _every_ install.** Live GitHub API, right now:

- `GET /repos/garrytan/gbrain/releases/latest` → **404** (unauthenticated *and* authenticated)
- `GET /repos/garrytan/gbrain/releases` → **200 `[]`** (zero published Releases; the repo has 1 git tag)

So `fetchLatestRelease()` returns `null` for everyone, not just source installs — `check-update` can never report an update until either (a) the repo starts cutting GitHub Releases, or (b) the check falls back to another signal. This is also the underlying cause of #486 (an npm / `package-json` install hitting the same `no_releases`): same empty source, different install method.

**New since this was filed — the blast radius grew.** The v0.42 self-upgrade work (#1798, "invocation-riding update check + opt-in auto-upgrade") **reuses `fetchLatestRelease()`** for its refresh path. So the new self-upgrade / auto-upgrade feature is built on a release lookup that always returns `null` for this repo — it's blind here too.

**Suggested fix** (matches option 1 above): repoint the latest-version signal at something actually populated on `garrytan/gbrain master` — e.g. `raw.githubusercontent.com/garrytan/gbrain/master/package.json` `.version`, or the top `## [x.y.z]` header in `CHANGELOG.md` (which `fetchChangelog()` already fetches). For source installs, the local-HEAD-vs-`origin/master` comparison suggested here also works.

**One latent follow-on** once the source is fixed: `isMinorOrMajorBump()` only flags minor/major (`0.X.0`) bumps, but gbrain's real cadence lives in the 3rd/4th version segment (e.g. `0.42.1` → `0.42.12`). After fixing the release source, most real updates would still be filtered out unless the comparison honors those segments.

The hardening intent is preserved: `--no-recurse-submodules` is still applied to both `clone` and `pull` (just appended after the subcommand, where git accepts it); the top-level `-c` SSRF flags (`http.followRedirects=false`, `protocol.file.allow=never`, `protocol.ext.allow=never`) are unchanged and still effective.

Confirming this bug also occurs on **Linux** (Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS, x86_64, kernel 6.17.0-29), not just macOS. So the scope of #1340 is broader than the original macOS report.

**Environment:**
- OS: Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS (Noble Numbat)
- Kernel: 6.17.0-29-generic
- Bun: 1.3.14 (latest as of 2026-06-04)
- gbrain: 0.42.3.0 (official binary at /usr/local/bin/gbrain)
- PGLite: 0.4.3
- Architecture: x86_64

**Reproduction:**
```
$ gbrain brainstorm "test idea" --limit 1 --no-save
PGLite failed to initialize its WASM runtime.
  This looks like a Bun vfs issue: `/$$bunfs/root` is read-only on
  your system, so PGLite cannot extract its pglite.data WASM payload.
  ...
  Original error: ENOENT: no such file or directory, open '/$bunfs/root/pglite.data'
```

`/$$bunfs/root` does not exist on Linux either, so PGLite fails the same way it does on older macOS.

**Workaround that works on Linux:**

Bun's vfs respects `BUN_TMPDIR` — pointing it at a regular fs path lets PGLite extract its WASM payload to the right place:

```bash
BUN_TMPDIR=/tmp gbrain brainstorm "test idea" --limit 1 --no-save
```

`gbrain doctor --fast` (which skips DB connection) works without the env var, but any command that calls `engine.connect()` (brainstorm, grade_takes, cycle, sync) requires `BUN_TMPDIR=/tmp` or a similar writable mount.

**Note:** The user-visible hint currently only mentions `bun upgrade` or running via Node. Neither of these resolved the issue on Linux Ubuntu 24.04 with the latest Bun (1.3.14). Suggest adding `BUN_TMPDIR=/tmp` to the hint as a third option, since the underlying vfs behavior is platform-specific and affects Linux too.

Update — I root-caused this properly. The trigger isn't concurrency (my earlier hypothesis), it's **mixed-case slugs**.

`putPage` runs `validateSlug` (→ lowercase) internally, but `addTag` / `upsertChunks` don't, and `importFromContent` passes the caller's original slug to all of them. So a mixed-case slug writes the page row under a lowercased key while `addTag` queries the original casing → `addTag failed: page not found` → the import rolls back and the slug is left unwritable.

That fully explains the "dirty slug, but a fresh slug works" symptom in the original report: the fresh slugs that worked happened to be lowercase; the failing ones (e.g. Lark/Feishu doc tokens, which are mixed-case base62) weren't.

Minimal repro:

```
echo body | gbrain capture --stdin --slug Mixed-CASE   # put_page failed: Page not found: Mixed-CASE
echo body | gbrain capture --stdin --slug mixed-case   # works
```

Fix in #1877 — normalizes the slug once at the `importFromContent` entry point, plus a regression test.

(The PGLite serve/CLI lock contention I mentioned is a separate, real concern, but not the cause of these failures.)

## Open speculation: what a real walk looks like on this brain (and why)

Grounded in the actual corpus shape (~350K pages), not a toy. The top-level domains by mass, roughly: a huge `concepts/` layer (~48K), a dense `people/` layer (~44K), an `atoms/` layer of distilled insights (~17K), then thick verticals for the institution's work (`yc/` ~15K), media + primary `sources/` (~28K combined), `civic/`, `companies/`, `meetings/`, `events/`, `books/`, `products/`, and a long tail of journals, places, orgs, projects. **No personal specifics below — only the structural shape matters for the algorithm.**

The reason this brain is a *good* substrate for traversal (and why single-hop LSD underuses it): the mass is lopsided. `concepts/` + `people/` + `atoms/` are ~30% of all pages and they're densely interlinked, so a near-anchor almost always lands in that gravity well. Single-hop LSD then picks a far page by raw embedding distance — which on this corpus repeatedly resolves to the *same handful* of maximally-distant prefixes. That's exactly the failure Garry hit in the live session: the close pairs kept repeating. The well is too deep; one jump can't escape its rim.

### Why a walk escapes the well
Anti-locality-from-the-whole-path (Fork B2) is the fix *specifically because* of this mass imbalance. Hop 1 leaves the dense core. Hop 2 is then scored as "far from the core AND far from where hop 1 landed" — so it can't fall back into the well, and it can't sit next to hop 1 either. The walk is forced to *spread*, and on a corpus with this much conceptual mass, the spread is where the non-obvious endpoints live.

### Three concrete example trajectories (illustrative, domain-level only)
These are the *shapes* I expect to be productive — written at the prefix/domain level so nothing personal leaks. The point is the **why** of each hop, not the specific pages.

**Walk 1 — institutional → biological → contemplative.**
`concepts/ (an org-design or selection idea, near the question)` → hop1 `concepts/ or sources/ (something from systems biology / evolutionary dynamics, far)` → hop2 `books/ or writings/ (a contemplative / philosophical text, far from both)`. *Why:* selection mechanisms recur in all three layers but are described in completely different vocabularies. The org-design page knows the *what*, the biology page knows the *mechanism*, the contemplative page knows the *cost to the individual being selected*. Colliding the endpoints (institution ↔ inner cost) with biology as the bridge produces the thing none of them says alone: what a selection system does to the selected. Single-hop would never connect an org page to a contemplative one — they're not near each other and neither is the "most distant" page from the other.

**Walk 2 — product/market → historical event → personal-craft.**
`companies/ or products/ (a market-structure observation)` → hop1 `events/ or sources/ (a historical confrontation / shutdown / regulatory moment, far)` → hop2 `concepts/ (a craft or aesthetic principle, far from both)`. *Why:* this is the "timing beats quality" insight from this morning's tweetstorm, but reached structurally. The market page supplies the bet, the historical-event page supplies the counter-move and the clock, and the craft page reframes "survival" as a question of taste/restraint rather than force. The intermediate event page is the *associative bridge that earns the leap* from market dynamics to craft — exactly the grounding string Fork D1 hands the generator.

**Walk 3 — interpersonal/relational → economic/incentive → media/narrative.**
`people/ or atoms/ (a relational pattern, distilled)` → hop1 `concepts/ (an incentive / game-theoretic structure, far)` → hop2 `media/ or civic/ (a public-narrative dynamic, far from both)`. *Why:* the same underlying mechanism — how a private dynamic scales into a public one — is invisible if you only read any one layer. The relational page is too intimate to generalize, the incentive page too abstract to feel, the media page too surface to explain itself. The walk threads private → structural → public and the endpoint collision (intimate pattern ↔ public narrative) is the kind of thing that reads as genuinely original because almost no one has both ends of that thread in the same head.

### What I actually expect the data to show (testable predictions)
1. **Endpoint novelty rises with depth, then plateaus.** N=2→3 should sharply increase mean endpoint-distance-from-seed; N=4+ probably hits diminishing returns on this corpus because after 3 anti-local hops you're already in the sparse tail where pages stop being *reachable* (Fork A bites). Prediction: optimal default `--walk-depth 3`.
2. **Hybrid reachability (Fork A3) will matter here, and link-primary will starve.** With this much mass in `concepts/`/`people/`/`atoms/`, the link graph is probably dense *inside* the core and sparse *across* domains — which is the exact opposite of what a walk needs (it wants cross-domain edges). So pure link-reachability will keep the walk trapped in the well; embedding-neighborhood reachability is what lets it jump domains. Prediction: **embedding-primary, link as a tiebreak/grounding signal**, not the reverse. (Worth the `avg(connection_count)` check the spec calls for — I'd bet cross-domain links are rare.)
3. **The inverted judge will reject more single-hop ideas than walk endpoints.** If the walk is doing its job, depth-3 endpoints should pass the "too coherent → reject" gate at a *higher* rate than depth-1, because they're genuinely less obvious. If they don't, the anti-locality objective is mis-tuned (probably stuck on max-from-seed instead of max-from-path).

### The honest risk
The thing that could make this a dud: if `concepts/`/`atoms/` are *so* semantically central that every walk, regardless of seed, drifts into the same far tail (say, the most distant journal or place pages), then walks collapse to a few stereotyped trajectories and we've just added cost. Mitigation is Fork B3 (temperature-weighted hop sampling) so two walks from the same seed diverge — but that trades reproducibility for diversity. My lean: ship deterministic (`--walk-temp 0`) first, measure trajectory collapse, turn on temperature only if the walks are too samey. That's a measurement, not a guess — the corpus is big and lopsided enough that I genuinely don't know which way it breaks, and that uncertainty is the reason to build it behind a flag and instrument the path distances from day one.

---
*Speculation added per request — grounded in the live corpus's domain distribution, personal specifics deliberately omitted. The domain-level walk shapes above are illustrative of the mechanism, not actual generated ideas.*

The immediate trigger was a single bad frontmatter title (#1939, fixed in #1944) — removing it stops the common case. But the structural issue you describe stands: a large-source full sync with **no intermediate `last_commit` checkpoint** can't converge if import time > session timeout. Intermediate checkpointing (advance `last_commit` to the last fully-imported commit boundary on SIGTERM) would make this self-healing rather than a permanent re-import loop.

Fixed. The queue-scoped DB singleton lock this issue called for shipped in **v0.42.29.0**, with a hardening follow-up in **v0.42.31.0**. Mapping to the three suggestions:

1. **Queue-scoped lock as the real singleton** — `supervisor.start()` now acquires a DB lock keyed on the queue (the database half of the mutex is physical — the lock row lives inside the target DB), so a second supervisor on the same `(database, queue)` fails fast with exit 2 regardless of `$HOME` or `--pid-file`. The lock refreshes on a dedicated timer and fails *safe* (exits non-zero) before the TTL could lapse and let a second supervisor take over.
2. **Canonical default pidfile** — derived from the brain id (config-only, no DB connect) instead of `$HOME`, so two brains under one `HOME` no longer share `supervisor.pid`.
3. **`doctor` observability** — a new `supervisor_singleton` check surfaces the effective `--max-rss` from the `started` audit event and warns when the lock holder's `(host, pid)` differs from the local pidfile holder.

The v0.42.31.0 follow-up fixed two bugs adversarial review caught in the original work: the lock key wrongly folded in a config-derived DB identity (so equivalent-but-different connection strings hashed differently and both acquired the "singleton"), now keyed on the queue alone; and the pidfile-cleanup `exit` listener was installed after the lock acquire, stranding the pidfile on the lock-held early-exit. Regression tests in `test/supervisor-db-lock.test.ts` pin both. Closing.

Corroborating data point — with a failure mode beyond the noise/cost angle already in this thread: a gitignored path doesn't just bloat the index, a single pathological file in there can **block the sync outright**.

On a repo that keeps ~1,300 generated backtest/report artifacts under a gitignored `artifacts/` directory, `gbrain sync` (first/full, `--strategy auto`) walked the entire `artifacts/` tree — it isn't `node_modules`/`ops`/dot-prefixed, so the current `collectSyncableFiles` skip-list doesn't catch it. Two consequences:

- **~17-minute walk** over the gitignored corpus on every full sync (it's all on disk, just untracked), which blew past the surrounding orchestration timeout → degraded run + rollback.
- **Hard parse failures**: ~105 of those artifacts were **UTF-16** `.htm` reports. The chunker hit `invalid byte sequence … 0x00` on them. This is the same "pathological gitignored file wedges the chunker" class noted earlier in this thread for giant single-line JSON — UTF-16 / binary-ish content is a second, common trigger (anything that emits UTF-16 reports: Windows-side test runners, some exporters).

So the cost isn't only DB bloat / embedding spend / polluted search — it's **sync reliability**. Gitignored generated output is exactly the content most likely to be large, binary-ish, or malformed, and walking it can fail the whole run.

This also reinforces the **descent-time prune** in #1159 over an emit-time filter: a fully-ignored `artifacts/` should never be *recursed into*, so neither the 17-minute walk nor the UTF-16 parse attempts ever happen.

(FWIW the `.gitignore` half of #1169 still reproduces on `master` @ v0.42.37 — the v0.37.7.0 fix addressed the submodule half via `pruneDir`, but `collectSyncableFiles` still admits gitignored on-disk files. Confirmed with a `--full --dry-run`: the file count drops by exactly the ignored set once the walker is filtered through `git ls-files --others --ignored --exclude-standard`.)

Happy to share a minimal repro or a regression test if it'd help move #1159 along.

## Workaround that resolved the issue

After exhausting other approaches (switching bun to stable build, trying Node.js instead), the fix was a **fresh install to a path with no special characters**:

```
C:\gbrain
```

Installing directly to a root-level directory outside the user profile entirely avoided the apostrophe in `C:\Users\Arnuv'\` and migrations completed successfully.

**Steps that did NOT help (save others the time):**
- Switching to a stable bun build
- Replacing bun with Node.js
- Running `gbrain apply-migrations --force-retry 0.12.0` (WEDGE recovery doesn't work while the path issue exists)

**Recommended workaround until the path is properly escaped:**
If your Windows username contains an apostrophe, install gbrain to a clean root path like `C:\gbrain` rather than the default user profile location.

Hit a second non-convergence mode in the same predicate on v0.42.37.0, worth fixing together: pages **untouched since before the extractor watermark** can never clear the `links_extracted_at < versionTs` arm, because `extractStaleFromDB` stamps with the page's *read* `updated_at_iso` (race-safe by design) — which for old pages is older than `LINK_EXTRACTOR_VERSION_TS`. So every `extract --stale` re-processes them and re-stamps the same pre-watermark value, forever (420/698 of our "stale" pages were this).

One-time data fix that cleared it for us (safe: only touches pages whose content hasn't changed since their last stamp):

```sql
UPDATE pages
   SET links_extracted_at = '<LINK_EXTRACTOR_VERSION_TS>'::timestamptz
 WHERE links_extracted_at IS NOT NULL
   AND links_extracted_at < '<LINK_EXTRACTOR_VERSION_TS>'::timestamptz
   AND updated_at <= links_extracted_at;
```

Durable fix suggestion: stamp with `GREATEST(read_updated_at, versionTs)` instead of the raw read value — keeps the race-safety property while letting the watermark arm converge. (Recurs on every future watermark bump otherwise.)

Nice fix — the root-cause framing is right. The real bug here isn't just "doesn't honor `.gitignore`," it's that `collectSyncableFiles` carried its own inline skip list (`node_modules || ops`) that drifted from the canonical `pruneDir()` gate and covered neither `vendor` nor anything else. Routing the FS fallback back through `pruneDir()` so the two can't diverge again is the part #1159 doesn't do, and adding `vendor`/`dist`/`build` to `PRUNE_DIR_NAMES` helps the incremental (`classifySync`) path too, not just the full walk. The Laravel 52,164 → 1,028 repro is a clean demonstration of the #1073 stall.

Worth noting for the maintainer's triage: like #1159, this adds **no npm dependency** — it shells out via `execFileSync('git', …)`, so the "requires the `ignore` package" concern that kept #1159 out of the v0.37.7.0 wave doesn't apply here either.

**One behavioral risk to flag:** this is **default-on** — whenever `dir` is a git work tree the walk switches to `git ls-files`, with no flag or config gate. That silently changes behavior for **dotfile/secret brains that deliberately `.gitignore` content but still want it brain-searchable** — the exact "why not just default-on?" case raised in #1073, which #1159 preserved by putting the behavior behind a default-off `--respect-gitignore` flag. Repos like this one clearly *want* the prune, but those brains would lose indexed content without opting in.

I don't have a strong opinion on how to resolve that — whether to blend the two (this PR's `pruneDir` dedupe + `PRUNE_DIR_NAMES` additions, gated behind #1159's opt-in flag), accept this one as-is and treat the secret-brain case as a follow-up, or pick one PR over the other — is entirely the maintainer's call, and it overlaps the in-flight #1942 vendor/dist/build prune as well. Just wanted the always-on tradeoff to be visible alongside the (real) improvements so it's a deliberate choice.

Same root cause, second instance — in the same file, on the layout axis rather than the language axis.

`runSkillifyCheckTarget()` hardwires a **nested** skills layout:

```ts
// src/commands/skillify-check.ts:194
const skillsDir = join(root, 'skills');
```

`root` comes from `projectRoot()` (lines 58–67), which walks up to the nearest `package.json`. A **flat** skills layout — `~/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` with no enclosing repo and no nested `skills/` subdir — has no `package.json`, so `root` falls back to `process.cwd()` and `skillsDir` resolves to `<cwd>/skills`, which doesn't exist. The two **required** items then both fail on every skill:

- `SKILL.md exists` (line 202) → looks at `<cwd>/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` (missing)
- `Resolver entry` (line 236) → `isInResolver()` looks under the same phantom dir

Result: exit 1 for every flat-layout skill regardless of how complete it is — the same "the work exists but the checker can't see it" failure this issue describes for Python tests.

And `--skills-dir` doesn't rescue it: `skillify check`'s `--help` (line 427) exposes only `[path] [--recent] [--json]`. The flag is parsed by `skillopt` (line 405), `check-resolvable`, and `skillpack`, but it never reaches `runSkillifyCheckTarget`, so there's no way to point the checker at a flat `skills/` root.

Repro:

```bash
cd ~/skills            # flat layout: ~/skills/<name>/SKILL.md, no nested skills/ subdir
gbrain skillify check <name>/scripts/<file>
# → SKILL.md exists: FAIL, Resolver entry: FAIL  (skillsDir = ~/skills/skills, nonexistent)
```

Suggests the fix here is the layout twin of the one above: either accept the target's own enclosing directory as the skills root when no nested `skills/` exists, or honor `--skills-dir` in `skillify check` the way the sibling commands already do.

Adding a related facet from a fresh deployment attempt on **Google Cloud SQL** (v0.42.40.0, Postgres 16):

On Cloud SQL, `BYPASSRLS` is not grantable at all — the platform reserves it, and even the default `postgres`/`cloudsqlsuperuser` roles don't hold it. Since fresh installs replay the migration ladder from v23, every new Cloud SQL deployment hard-fails at:

```
[24] rls_backfill_missing_tables...
Schema probe failed: v24 rls_backfill_missing_tables: role <user> does not have BYPASSRLS privilege — cannot enable RLS safely. Re-run as postgres (or another BYPASSRLS role).
```

There is no "re-run as postgres" that works on this platform. (Getting past v24 by other means then hits v35 `auto_rls_event_trigger`, which needs full superuser for `CREATE EVENT TRIGGER` — also unavailable on Cloud SQL.)

Worth noting the embedded base schema already handles the no-BYPASSRLS case gracefully (its DO block skips enabling RLS with a NOTICE, *"otherwise we'd lock ourselves out"*). A similar graceful skip — or an explicit `--no-rls` opt-out for managed-Postgres platforms where the anon-key threat model doesn't apply — would make Cloud SQL (and likely RDS/Azure equivalents) viable targets. We worked around it by self-hosting Postgres 16 on the same VM where BYPASSRLS+superuser are grantable.

Hit this exact inversion class on a personal brain (0.42.38.0, Postgres, ~330 pages) and traced it to two compounding mechanisms — posting since both have concrete fixes.

**1. The recency boost is upward-multiplicative and ungated by default.** `applyRecencyBoost` computes `score *= 1 + coefficient × halflife/(halflife + age)`. Your trace shows the signature: every stale-but-fresh-`updated_at` page wearing a large factor while the true hit (`people/zhangsan`, base-relevant) sits unboosted at the bottom. Two corpus-level traps make it bite:

- `DEFAULT_FALLBACK` is `{halflifeDays: 90, coefficient: 0.5}` — any page whose slug matches **no prefix** in `DEFAULT_RECENCY_DECAY` gets a bigger boost ceiling (×1.5, or ×1.75 under `recency='strong'`) than most mapped families. On my corpus, freshly-touched unmapped pages (`memory`, top-level notes) leapfrogged a diary page with a *higher* base score (0.81 vs 0.77 pre-boost → 1.15 vs 1.34 post-boost). If you tune any per-prefix coefficients down, the untouched fallback silently becomes the strongest boost in the system.
- Age uses `COALESCE(effective_date, updated_at, created_at)` — so frequently-edited evergreen pages are perpetually "fresh" and collect the boost forever.

**2. The shipped mitigation exists but is off by default.** v0.35.6.0's floor-ratio gate (#1091/#1129) skips all post-fusion boosts for results whose base score < `floorRatio × top base` — exactly the "weak page climbs over the legitimate primary hit" failure. It's `undefined` in all three mode bundles.

What fixed it for me, verified against a 26-query gold fixture (one family went 67%→100% Hit@3):

```
gbrain config set search.floor_ratio 0.9   # 0.85–0.95 band for dense embedders, per #1091
```

plus lowering `DEFAULT_FALLBACK.coefficient` below the most conservative mapped family (0.5 → 0.1 in my fork).

Possible upstream moves, in increasing ambition: flip a conservative `floor_ratio` default on in the mode bundles (the per-corpus ablation in TODOS.md gates this, per the code comments); clamp `DEFAULT_FALLBACK.coefficient` to `min` of the mapped families at resolve time; or longer-term make recency a downward decay from 1.0 (Elasticsearch `function_score` convention: stale sinks, fresh never exceeds its base relevance) — that shape makes this whole inversion class unrepresentable.

## Follow-up: investigated the "158M new tokens" — it's a phantom. The gate estimate is a full-tree ceiling, not a delta.

Dug into why a routine daily sync was pricing ~158M tokens / $7.91. **The actual new content was 336 files → 287 chunks (~0.5M chars, ~$0.04).** The estimate was off by ~400x.

### Root cause: `estimateInlineNewTokens` prices the whole tree for any "changed" source

Per the v0.41.31 comment in sync.ts: a source contributes ZERO only when *provably unchanged* (HEAD == last_commit AND **clean working tree** AND chunker_version match). Otherwise it contributes the **full-tree ceiling** — every char of every file in the source.

On an active brain the primary source is *never* "unchanged" (agents/crons write to the working tree constantly; the tree is rarely git-clean at sync time). So the gate prices the entire ~550M-char corpus on every sync:

```
~158,200,000 "new tokens", est. $7.91   <- whole tree
actual delta this sync: 336 files, 287 chunks  <- ~$0.04
```

Verified via direct SQL: only **654 chunks (1.1M chars)** have NULL embeddings; signature drift is small. There was never an $8 embed pending — the blocking gate was defending against a number ~400x larger than reality, every day, wedging the cron each time.

### Why this matters beyond the wedge

- Operator sees "~158M new tokens ($7.91)" and reasonably suspects runaway ingestion — costly false alarm.
- Using a full-tree *ceiling* as the **blocking trigger** means any actively-written source permanently gates at its corpus size. The gate can never pass on a busy brain without --yes.

### Suggested fix (priority order)

1. **Estimate the delta, not the tree**: git diff --stat last_commit..HEAD (plus dirty files) gives changed paths; price only those. content_hash short-circuiting already guarantees unchanged files cost $0 at execution — the *estimate* should match execution semantics.
2. If a cheap delta estimate isn't possible, label honestly ("<=158M tokens, full-tree ceiling — unchanged files skip via content_hash") and block on a measured post-import chunk count instead (sync knows exactly how many chunks it created before embedding starts).
3. The earlier asks (tokenmax posture, 0/off support, non-TTY defer) still stand — but fixing the estimator removes ~99% of false gate fires for everyone.

### Environment
- gbrain 0.42.39.0, 193K pages / 373K chunks / ~500M chars, 4 sources, daily sync cron
- Actual stale state: 654 NULL-embedding chunks (1.1M chars) via direct SQL

Note: #2044 is the primary *accrual source* for the unbounded `row_num`-NULL backlog in #1867. A deposit onto an already-fenced page collides on `idx_facts_fence_key` here, the fence write rolls back, and the fact silently falls back to a DB-only insert (`row_num` NULL). Making the fence write idempotent here would stop most of #1867's growth at the source. Production accrual numbers + the traced fence-first fallback are on #1867.

### Real-world impact + reproduction (from a production single-user brain)

Confirming this bites normal use, with numbers and a precise mechanism, in case it helps triage.

**Observed accrual under ordinary use** (default source *with* a `local_path`, not thin-client):
`row_num IS NULL` count grew 397 (Jun 1) → 707 (Jun 4) → 708 (Jun 6) → **754 (Jun 14)** — ~40–50/week, purely from day-to-day `extract_facts` deposits.

**Mechanism (traced to `core/facts/backstop.ts`):** the deposit path is fence-first and falls back to a DB-only insert (`row_num` NULL) when the fence write fails. The dominant trigger is **#2044**: depositing onto an entity page that *already* has a `## Facts` fence collides on `idx_facts_fence_key`, the fence write is rolled back, and the fact silently lands DB-only. So the busiest pages (the ones with the most facts) are the ones that keep shedding un-fenced facts. Facts with no resolved `entity_slug` take the same DB-only fallback.

**Why it never self-heals:** there is no re-fence sweep, and the only backfill (`v0_32_2`) is gated by the migration ledger's "complete never regresses" rule — `apply-migrations --force-retry` is ignored once it's recorded complete (it originally ran on a brain with zero facts, fencing nothing). So nothing ever recovers the DB-only fallbacks.

**Consequence:** stranded facts stay queryable via `recall` but are **not** in the system-of-record markdown — they're dropped by `gbrain rebuild` and never graph-attach to their page.

**Suggested directions (either solves most of it):**
1. Make the deposit-time fence write **idempotent** (fixes #2044 → removes the main accrual source).
2. Ship a **re-runnable re-fence** (e.g. `gbrain extract facts --refence` or an idempotent `v0_32_2` re-run) that walks `row_num IS NULL` rows and fences them — so existing/legacy stranded facts can be recovered without hand-surgery.

Workaround we used to drain a 754-fact backlog: normalize entity slugs → fence → reconcile, with two gotchas worth documenting (the fence write must be followed by a sync before the `extract_facts` reconcile, or the reconcile reads fence-less DB content and deletes facts; and #2044 must be worked around per-page).

Endorse — and another concrete data point that argues for **keying the exclusion off the type's `primitive`, not a hardcoded slug list**.

On an atom-heavy brain (`gbrain 0.42.44.0`, base pack `gbrain-base-v2`):

```
orphan_ratio: 87% (2558/2940 linkable)

Of the 2558 orphans:
  atoms (type: atom):   1602   (63%)
  everything else:       956
```

The dominant offender here isn't `code`/`calendar`/`m365-*` — it's `atom`, which the base pack itself defines as a leaf node:

```yaml
- name: atom
  primitive: annotation     # not entity, not concept
  extractable: false        # atoms are extraction OUTPUT, not a link source
```

`cycle/extract-atoms.ts` writes each atom with `source_slug` (or `source_path`) as **frontmatter provenance only** — it creates zero graph edges. And the pack's `page_to_link` rules materialize edges *only* for relationship atoms (`atom-partner-link` / `partner-atom-link`); ordinary `extraction`/`manual`/`lore` atoms are just retyped to `atom` with no source→atom edge. So by design, every ordinary atom is born an orphan and nothing in the pipeline is ever meant to link to it. They're retrieved by embedding/semantic search, not graph traversal.

This is the same composition bias #1144 describes, but it means the hardcoded raw-ingest list from the comment above (`code, calendar-event, m365-*, imessage, ...`) still wouldn't touch my dominant offender — `atom` isn't on it, and it won't be on the next person's list either.

**Suggestion:** rather than (or in addition to) a slug allow/deny list, exclude by **primitive** — `annotation` pages are leaf-by-definition and shouldn't count as orphan candidates at all. That's drift-proof: any future ingest type declared with `primitive: annotation` (or a similar "leaf" primitive) is automatically handled without editing the list. The Option 3 `GBRAIN_BRAIN_SCORE_TYPES` env override is still the right long-term escape hatch; a primitive-based default just makes the out-of-the-box number trustworthy for atom/annotation-heavy brains.

(Separately relevant for anyone landing here: the doctor's remediation hint `extract links --by-mention` can't clear this regardless — see #2043. On my brain it created 348 mention edges and moved orphan_ratio by exactly 1 page, since the mention linker only targets `person/company/organization/entity` and never atoms.)

Hit this independently (v0.42.37.0, Postgres/Neon) via the gstack memory-ingest stage, which imports transcripts into the schema-default source with no `--source`. Adding a precise code-level root cause, because there's a real logic inconsistency here, not only a UX/config gap.

The proximate cause is that the two "no `sourceId`" fallbacks resolve differently:

- `import-file.ts:561` computes existence with
  `const existing = await engine.getPage(slug, sourceId ? { sourceId } : undefined)`.
  In `postgres-engine.ts` `getPage`, when `sourceId`/`sourceIds` are both undefined the source filter is an **empty fragment** — so the lookup is global by slug (`WHERE slug = $1 AND deleted_at IS NULL LIMIT 1`) and returns whichever source's row Postgres yields first.
- `import-file.ts:733` then does `if (existing) await tx.createVersion(slug, txOpts)` with `txOpts = sourceId ? { sourceId } : undefined`.
- `postgres-engine.ts:4538` `createVersion` resolves `const sourceId = opts?.sourceId ?? 'default'` and queries `WHERE slug = $1 AND source_id = 'default'` → 0 rows → `createVersion failed: page "<slug>" (source=default) not found`.

So for a slug that exists under a non-default source, an unscoped import sees `existing = true` (global match) but tries to version it under `default` (literal fallback) and throws — instead of inserting a new `(default, slug)` row, which `pages_source_slug_key UNIQUE (source_id, slug)` permits.

The two fallbacks should agree. Minimal fix: scope the existence check to the same default the write uses, e.g. `engine.getPage(slug, { sourceId: sourceId ?? 'default' })` at `import-file.ts:561`. Then an unscoped import of a slug owned by another source resolves `existing = null` and inserts cleanly, rather than colliding.

Same divergence exists in `pglite-engine.ts` (`createVersion` at :4466, throw at :4475).

Secondary, orthogonal: `gbrain import` returns a non-zero exit whenever `errors > 0` even with `status: "success"` and `imported: 0`, so a batch importer that can't gate per-file state books the whole batch as failed on a single stuck page.

This patch fixes several bugs/footguns I hit while testing facts extraction against real conversation-style turns and private/OpenAI-compatible provider routing.

### 1. `facts.extraction_model` could be configured but extraction still silently no-oped

Before this PR, `extractFactsFromTurn()` checked:

```ts
isAvailable('chat')
```

before resolving the effective facts extraction model. That means availability was tested against the global/default chat model, not the model actually used for facts extraction.

Failure mode:

- global/default chat model points at provider A
- `facts.extraction_model` points at provider B
- provider A is not configured/available
- provider B is configured/available
- extraction returns `[]` before it ever calls chat

This is especially visible for local/private/OpenAI-compatible routing, where a user may want facts extraction to use one local/private model while leaving the global chat model alone.

Fix in this PR:

- resolve `const model = input.model ?? await getFactsExtractionModel(input.engine)` first
- test `isAvailable('chat', model)` against that effective model
- pass the same effective model into `chat()`

### 2. `provider_base_urls.<provider>` was accepted as config but not merged into runtime gateway config

`gbrain config set provider_base_urls.openrouter http://...` is allowed by the known config-key prefix, but `loadConfigWithEngine()` was not reading/merging those DB-plane prefixed keys into `provider_base_urls`.

Failure mode:

- user configures an OpenAI-compatible local/private endpoint via `provider_base_urls.openrouter`
- config write succeeds
- gateway config never sees that base URL after engine merge
- facts extraction/provider tests can still route to the default provider URL or appear unavailable

Fix in this PR:

- if the engine supports `listConfigKeys`, load keys under `provider_base_urls.`
- merge them into `merged.provider_base_urls`
- keep file-plane config precedence over DB-plane values

### 3. Obvious non-memory turns were still sent to the LLM extractor

The prompt tells the model to skip questions/operational chatter, but in practice this is exactly the class of thing that benefits from deterministic filtering before the model call.

Failure mode:

- exact-reply probes, smoke tests, short acks, and ordinary task requests go to the LLM
- weaker/local models sometimes convert them into durable facts/commitments
- unnecessary model calls add latency/cost and create hot-memory noise

Fix in this PR:

- add a conservative `shouldSkipTurnForFactsExtraction()` pre-filter
- skip pure acks, exact-reply/smoke-test probes, wrappers, and ordinary task/question turns
- preserve turns with durable preference/rule markers such as `I prefer`, `make sure`, `always`, `never`, `source of truth`, etc.

### 4. Kind classification was too model-dependent for common high-signal first-person markers

In real conversation turns, the model may extract the right text but assign a weak/wrong kind, especially for local/private models.

Examples:

- `I prefer ...` should be `preference`
- `make sure ...`, `we decided ...`, `always/never/do not ...` should generally be `commitment`
- `I think/I believe ...` should be `belief`
- typed metric assertions should remain `fact`

Fix in this PR:

- add `normalizeExtractedFactKind()` as a deterministic post-guard around model output
- force typed metric claims to `fact`
- normalize obvious preference/commitment/belief markers

### 5. Multi-claim turns could smear one marker across unrelated extracted facts

A turn can contain both a preference and a decision, e.g.:

```text
I prefer concise extraction candidates. I decided to use a private model for facts extraction.
```

A naive whole-turn normalizer would see `decided` and mark both facts as `commitment`.

Fix in this PR:

- prefer evidence in the extracted fact text itself
- only fall back to whole-turn evidence when the turn has a single unambiguous marker class
- added a regression test so the preference stays `preference` and the decision stays `commitment`

### Test coverage added

The PR adds targeted coverage for:

- transient pre-filter skips before chat is called
- durable style/rule feedback is not skipped
- high-signal kind normalization
- multi-claim kind-smear prevention
- facts-model availability independent of global chat model
- DB-plane `provider_base_urls.<provider>` runtime merge
- file-plane provider base URL precedence

## Update — two deeper bugs found while remediating a stuck large-delta sync

Investigating a source whose `last_sync_at` was frozen ~76h despite the queue/supervisor being healthy, found two issues beyond the concurrency cap:

### Bug A — `sync-target` op-checkpoint recurs as a JSONB scalar (crashes checkpoint load every sync)

On a large-delta sync (~6,700 changed files: ~2,000 deletes, ~1,500 renames, ~280 imports), the resume-checkpoint loader throws on every run:

```
[op-checkpoint] load failed (sync-target, <fp>): cannot extract elements from a scalar
```

Root: the `op_checkpoints` row for `op='sync-target'` has `completed_keys` stored as a JSONB **string scalar** instead of an **array**, so the loader's `jsonb_array_elements_text(completed_keys)` blows up. Confirmed via:

```sql
SELECT fingerprint, jsonb_typeof(completed_keys) FROM op_checkpoints WHERE op='sync-target';
-- => type 'string' (should be 'array')
```

Manually repairing it (`SET completed_keys='[]'::jsonb WHERE jsonb_typeof(completed_keys)<>'array'`) clears the crash — but it **recurs**: after one subsequent sync of the large-delta source, the row is a scalar again. So a write path in the sync/checkpoint code is persisting `completed_keys` as a scalar on this code path. `recordCompleted()` looks correct (`JSON.stringify(sorted)` of an array → proper array). The recurring corruption suggests a different writer (or a `$3::jsonb` cast receiving a bare string somewhere in the sync-target pin path). Worth auditing every write to `op_checkpoints.completed_keys` for sync-target specifically.

Suggested hardening regardless of root cause: a CHECK constraint or a defensive coalesce so a scalar can never be stored (`completed_keys` should be NOT NULL DEFAULT `'[]'::jsonb` with `jsonb_typeof = 'array'` enforced), and the loader should treat a non-array as empty rather than throwing.

### Bug B — the rename phase is sequential and dominates large-delta wall time

`--workers N` parallelizes the import phase, but the **rename phase** (slug updates for moved files) is a plain sequential `for ... await updateSlug` loop. On a ~1,500-file directory move it runs ~3–4s per rename single-threaded, i.e. ~90 min wall — and it runs BEFORE the parallel import phase, so `--workers` does nothing for it. On a large reorg (bulk dir move), renames are the dominant cost, not imports. Renames are independent slug updates and look batchable / parallelizable the same way imports are.

### Interaction with the original report

These compound the single-core issue: a large-delta sync (a) crashes its resume checkpoint so it can't skip already-done work, and (b) spends most of its time in a sequential rename loop on one core. Combined with the daemon path not engaging the worker pool, a big reorg can leave a source's `last_sync_at` frozen for days while each attempt does partial work and never reaches the final commit-anchor write that stamps `last_sync_at`.

**Update: this is blocked on a deeper bug.** See #2238.

Investigation found that sync is single-core-bound at the **database layer**, not the queue layer. The `pages` table has a statement-level trigger (`bump_page_generation_clock_trg`) that does `UPDATE page_generation_clock SET value = value + 1 WHERE id = 1` on every INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE. `page_generation_clock` is a single-row table, so every concurrent writer takes a `RowExclusiveLock` on that one tuple and serializes on commit.

Caught live: 8 parallel `import` processes → 18 connections stuck on `Lock/transactionid`, all queued on `page_generation_clock`, total throughput 0.8-0.9 cores / ~0.64 pages/sec. Not CPU-bound — commit-serialized on one row.

So adding core-aware worker concurrency (this issue) cannot help until that global serialization point is removed — the workers will still queue on one row. The fix order in #2238 is: batch the page writes (clock bumps once per batch, not per file) and/or swap the locked-row counter for a sequence, **then** worker-pool the queue sync path. This issue should land on top of that work.

Confirming this on a live Postgres-backed brain (Supabase session pooler, v0.42.51.0). Same failure, same root cause, and the proposed `to_jsonb($3::text[])` fix is verified working here.

**Repro / blast radius**
- `gbrain sync` aborts before import on any source with pending files: `0 of N file(s) imported, reason=checkpoint_unavailable`, preceded by `[op-checkpoint] write failed (sync-target, …): new row for relation "op_checkpoints" violates check constraint "op_checkpoints_completed_keys_array"`.
- The `(pool unavailable)` text in the abort line is misleading — the pool is fine; it's the CHECK rejecting the row.
- The autopilot daemon loops on the same failure every tick (sync jobs never advance `last_commit`).
- `op_checkpoints` was **empty**, so this is the *first* `sync-target` write. Sources that are already up-to-date never write a target checkpoint, so they appear unaffected until something changes on disk.

**Mechanism (confirmed against the live DB)**
The `sync-target` write goes through `recordCompleted()` → `INSERT … $3::jsonb` with `JSON.stringify([pin])`. On postgres.js that lands as a JSON *string* scalar, not an array:

```sql
SELECT jsonb_typeof('["abc"]'::jsonb)            -- array   (passes CHECK)
SELECT jsonb_typeof(to_jsonb('["abc"]'::text))   -- string  (fails CHECK)
```

PGLite hides the double-encode, which is why CI is green and why the inline comment in `recordCompleted` asserts the `$3::jsonb` form is safe. The migration-119 `CHECK (jsonb_typeof(completed_keys) = 'array')` turns the previously-silent corruption into a hard insert failure on Postgres — working as designed; it just exposed an existing write-path bug.

**Note:** `gbrain doctor` does not surface this — it reports a healthy score while sync silently fails. A `sync_freshness`/checkpoint probe that notices `last_commit` not advancing despite disk changes would catch it.

**Fix (matches the proposal)**
Mirror the safe `appendCompleted` / `APPEND_PATHS_SQL` pattern — bind the JS `string[]` as a Postgres `text[]` and let the server build the jsonb array:

```diff
- VALUES ($1, $2, $3::jsonb, now())             … JSON.stringify(sorted)
+ VALUES ($1, $2, to_jsonb($3::text[]), now())  … sorted
```

(the `ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE SET completed_keys = EXCLUDED.completed_keys` path inherits the fix). The stale comment claiming the old form is safe should be updated, since it's only true on PGLite.

**Verified:** with the patch, sync imported all pending files in one pass, links/timeline extracted, and the autopilot cron is green. Happy to send a PR.

**Workaround applied in production** (gbrain 0.42.44.0, external Postgres):

Parameter-free, server-side unwrap — preserves all keys and can't be re-encoded by the driver:

```sql
UPDATE sources
SET config = (config #>> '{}')::jsonb
WHERE jsonb_typeof(config) = 'string';
```

After this, `config->>'github_repo'` resolves and `POST /webhooks/github` returns `202 {job_id,…}` instead of `404 unknown_repo`.

**Caveat — it's not durable.** Any later config-writing CLI command (`sources federate`, `sources webhook set`, `sources rename`, …) re-introduces the double-encoding via the `UPDATE … config = $1::jsonb` + `JSON.stringify(cfg)` path, so the unwrap has to be re-run afterward. A `jsonb_build_object('webhook_secret', $1::text, 'github_repo', $2::text)` write also yields a correct object, but is likewise clobbered by the next CLI write — which is why the real fix belongs in the persist path itself.

**Workaround applied in production** (containerized deploy — Docker/Coolify):

Bypassed the supervisor entirely and run a **self-restarting bare worker loop** in the container entrypoint, since `gbrain jobs work` takes no singleton lease:

```bash
( while true; do gbrain jobs work; echo "[gbrain] worker exited rc=$? — restarting in 5s"; sleep 5; done ) &
```

This survives redeploys cleanly — there's no `gbrain_cycle_locks` supervisor lease to go stale across a hostname change.

Additionally pinned the container hostname (`hostname: gbrain-drich` in compose) so that any **per-job** lock (`gbrain-sync`, etc.) left behind by an abruptly-killed container is classified same-host and taken over after the 60s grace, instead of waiting out the TTL.

Live proof: run_doctor returned skill category 100/100 while list_skills could not find the skills dir at all. Fix that one behavior and Bugs 1 (MCP check-set divergence) and 2 (unfixable resolver FAIL) surface honestly on their own. Bug 3 (get_health 1385 vs get_stats 915) is a separate MCP-vs-MCP divergence. MCP surface reproduced live; CLI 70/15 figures are operator-reported.

## Root-cause refinement (corrects my earlier TL;DR)

After reading the source, my first comment was imprecise. Bug 0 is **not** an accidental "omitted checks score as PASS" defect — it's an **intentional contract that breaks on the MCP/remote surface**. Worth getting exact since it changes the fix.

### The mechanism

`_penaltyScore([])` returns `100` (`src/commands/doctor.ts:143`). An empty category therefore scores a perfect 100, and that is **deliberately pinned**:

```ts
// test/doctor-brain-checks-score.test.ts:132
test('empty category gets 100 (vacuous truth)', () => {
  const r = computeDoctorReport([check('brain_score', 'ok')]);
  expect(r.category_scores.skill).toBe(100);  // no skill checks ran
});
```

The design comment (`doctor.ts:122-127`) confirms intent: categories were decoupled so `brain` stays ~100 when `skill` is polluted by RESOLVER warnings. The assumption baked in is **every category always has checks**.

### Why it produces a false "healthy" over MCP

That assumption holds locally but is violated remotely:

- **Local `gbrain doctor`** — skill checks (`resolver_health`, `skill_conformance`, …) always run, so `category_scores.skill: 100` honestly means *all skill checks passed*.
- **MCP `run_doctor` / remote** — ships a deliberately focused subset (`doctor.ts:197-212`) that **omits the entire skill check group**. So `skill: []` → vacuous `100`.

Live repro on my brain (gbrain 0.42.43.0, via MCP): `run_doctor` returned `category_scores.skill: 100` **at the same moment** `list_skills` returned `storage_error: No skills directory found on the server host`. A perfect skill score on a tree the host can't even read. The vacuous-truth rule and the focused-subset omission only lie **in combination**.

### Two fixes (not a clean one-line patch — this touches a pinned contract)

**A — honesty guard (narrow):** report `category_scores.{cat}: null` ("not assessed") when a category has zero checks, instead of `100`. Overturns the `vacuous truth` test, needs a guard in the human printer (`doctor.ts:7527` prints `${...skill}/100`), and a type change to `number | null`. Small, but it *is* a contract change.

**B — fix at the surface (root):** MCP `run_doctor` runs the skill check group too, OR explicitly declares itself a subset and bubbles any FAIL-level check from the full set. This makes the vacuous-100 moot because skill checks would actually run. Bigger, but kills the divergence at source.

**Recommendation:** B is the real fix; A is a cheap honesty backstop worth shipping regardless (any future skipped category — e.g. `--scope` gating — would otherwise re-introduce a vacuous 100). Happy to send a patch + test for whichever direction you prefer.

### Unchanged from the issue body
- Bug 3 (`get_health` 1385 pages vs `get_stats` 915, zeroed coverage) is independent of the above.
- MCP surface reproduced live; CLI 70/15 figures are operator-reported.

## Direction-A patch ready (not yet PR'd — want your call on A vs B first)

I have a tested honesty-guard patch in hand. Holding the PR because this touches a **deliberately pinned contract** (`empty category gets 100 (vacuous truth)`), so your call on direction before I open it.

Make `category_scores.{cat}` report `null` ("not assessed") for a category with zero checks, instead of a vacuous `100`. `brain_checks_score` stays numeric (preserves the byte-identical back-compat invariant).

This branch now carries three related fixes, verified locally on both PGLite and Postgres 17:

**1. MiniMax full-stack (original commits)** — embeddings compat shim (`input`->`texts`, `vectors`->`data[]`), asymmetric `type: db|query`, and a MiniMax-M3 chat touchpoint. Runs embeddings + think/dream/synthesis on MiniMax with no OpenAI/Anthropic key.

## Re-confirmed live after v0.42.52.0 — this is NOT a false alarm

v0.42.52.0 (#2287) reintroduced `$3::jsonb` in `recordCompleted` with a code comment asserting it is correct ("JSON.stringify into `$3::jsonb` is correct ... NOT the double-encode trap"). That assertion is empirically false against a real Postgres pool. Running a multi-source sync on that exact build:

```
[op-checkpoint] write failed (sync-target, 4f21bbc1): new row for relation "op_checkpoints" violates check constraint "op_checkpoints_completed_keys_array"
[sync] checkpoint target write failed (pool unavailable) — aborting before import; nothing drained, next run retries.
Sync PARTIAL: imported 0 of 4682 file(s), reason=checkpoint_unavailable.
```

The reason `recordCompleted` differs from the working `appendCompleted`: `appendCompleted` binds a `text[]` and does `unnest($3::text[])`, so the array is constructed server-side. `recordCompleted` binds a single JS **string** (`JSON.stringify(sorted)`) to a `$3::jsonb` param. Under postgres.js `.unsafe()`, a string bound to `::jsonb` takes the `text → jsonb` cast path, which produces a jsonb **scalar string** (`"[...]"`), not a jsonb array — failing `CHECK (jsonb_typeof(completed_keys) = 'array')`.

Forcing the param to bind as text first (`$3::text::jsonb`) makes the cast parse the JSON into a real array. Verified: straylight-brain (4682 files) syncs clean immediately after the cast change; reverts to the constraint failure without it.

Suggest also deleting/correcting the inline comment defending `$3::jsonb`, since it will invite another revert.

**Why this matters beyond our own use.** MQL4/MQL5 (MetaTrader) is one of the most widely deployed retail-trading languages, yet it has no dedicated tree-sitter grammar and — as far as we can find — no call-graph code-intelligence in any tool. Tagging `.mq4/.mq5/.mqh` as `mql` over the already-shipped tree-sitter-cpp grammar makes gbrain (to our knowledge) the first to give `code_callers`/`code_callees`/`code_blast`/`code_flow` over an MQL corpus — net-new language coverage at zero grammar-maintenance cost.

The enabling **C++ receiver-type resolution** also benefits plain C++ for the common shapes (non-namespaced classes; implicit-self, out-of-line, and value/pointer member-field or local-object receivers). Namespaced classes and reference-typed receivers aren't resolved yet — disclosed under **Known limitations**; they stay bare (no false edges) and don't affect MQL.

**Precision, measured:** on a real multi-file MQL corpus, 165 qualified call edges, 100% resolving to a real definition, **0 false edges** — globals and overloads stay deliberately bare rather than inventing confident-but-wrong edges. All TDD; engine match shares one regex + guard across PGLite and Postgres.

*Authored with AI assistance (Claude, plus a cross-model Codex review pass) under the contributor's direction.*

**Impact scope.** This isn't a marginal fix — the `completed_keys` double-encode blocks **100% of Postgres sync** (0 files imported, `last_commit` never advances, every retry re-fails the same checkpoint write), so any Postgres-backed gbrain is stuck until it lands. PGLite hides it (different driver path), which is why it slipped past.

It also surfaces a guard gap: `scripts/check-jsonb-pattern.sh` catches the template-literal `${JSON.stringify(x)}::jsonb` form but not the parameterized `.unsafe()` + `{ prepare: false }` twin this PR fixes. Extending that guard to the parameterized form would prevent the next instance (happy to follow up).

### Independent repro — confirmed on Supabase + Bun

Hit this on `gbrain 0.42.52.0` against a managed **Supabase** Postgres (Supavisor pooler), runtime **Bun 1.3.14**, **postgres.js 3.4.9**. Every `gbrain sync` of a source *with changes* aborted before import:

```
[op-checkpoint] write failed (sync-target, b4895013): new row for relation "op_checkpoints" violates check constraint "op_checkpoints_completed_keys_array"
[sync] checkpoint target write failed (pool unavailable) — aborting before import; nothing drained, next run retries.
Sync PARTIAL at c1dbf3c4: imported 0 of 1 file(s), reason=checkpoint_unavailable.
```

Sources with **0 changes** synced fine (they never reach the pin write), which is what masks it at first.

Isolated the binding against the live DB to rule out anything app-side:

```js
// payload = JSON.stringify(['x']) === '["x"]'
sql.unsafe(`SELECT jsonb_typeof($1::jsonb) t`, [payload])  // -> { t: 'string' }  ❌ scalar
sql`SELECT jsonb_typeof(${payload}::jsonb) t`              // -> { t: 'string' }  ❌ scalar (template too)
sql.unsafe(`SELECT jsonb_typeof('["x"]'::jsonb) t`)        // -> { t: 'array'  }  ✅ literal only
```

So under this runtime *both* the positional `.unsafe()` form and the template form double-encode — the inline comment in `recordCompleted` asserting the positional form is safe is empirically false here, confirming your note about deleting it before it invites another revert.

Verified both proposed fixes resolve it (rollback-tx test, then full sync):
- this PR's `$3::text::jsonb`
- the `to_jsonb($3::text[])` variant (matches the `appendCompleted` text[] path)

Both produce `jsonb_typeof = 'array'` and the sync drains cleanly. 👍 for getting one of these merged — the duplicate-PR pile suggests it's biting a lot of people.

A small/date-targeted synthesize canary had succeeded earlier, so this is not simply cron timing or the Hermes wrapper timeout.

This looks like the PGLite synthesize queue hang is still reachable in 0.42.52.0 despite the inline worker path in `runPgliteSubagentsInline(...)`: large fanouts can still leave the private `dream-inline-*` queue stranded and the cycle lock stale until the parent process is killed by an external timeout.

Useful direction: the daily/full-cycle path probably needs one of:

- bounded/resumable synthesize fanout instead of submitting hundreds of children in one cycle,
- a reliable PGLite inline drain that cannot leave private queues orphaned,
- cycle-level progress/timeout surfacing that returns a partial report instead of timing out with no child summary,
- or a CLI-level cap/window (`--max-transcripts`, `--max-children`, etc.) for scheduled dream runs.

### Still reproduces on **0.42.1.0** (`eefe8b5`) — same `reconnect()` → module-singleton null path, now also taking down the in-cycle `sync` phase

Confirming this is still open on **gbrain 0.42.1.0** (HEAD `eefe8b5741c27e59bf65198d46e3dfe5bfa70ce9`), two minor versions past the 0.41.28 report. Root cause matches exactly; adding fresh evidence in case it helps prioritize a durable fix.

#### Environment
- gbrain 0.42.1.0 (`eefe8b5`), Bun 1.3.14, macOS arm64
- Supabase Postgres, ~4,660 pages, pgvector, `text-embedding-3-large` @ 1536 dims
- **Reproduces on both** the direct connection (`db.<ref>.supabase.co:5432`) **and** the Session-mode pooler (`aws-1-<region>.pooler.supabase.com:5432`, user `postgres.<ref>`). Switching to the Session pooler had zero effect — this is not the Transaction-vs-Session `.begin()` issue.

#### Symptom (full `gbrain dream`, not just `--source`)
On every full cycle, **both** `sync` and `synthesize` fail; the other ~19 phases succeed. Cycle returns `partial`, `cycle_freshness` never clears, and `gbrain doctor` health score is permanently gated at 0 despite a fully functional brain.
```
sync       → {"class":"InternalError","code":"UNKNOWN","message":"No database connection: connect() has not been called. ..."}
synthesize → {"class":"InternalError","code":"SYNTH_PHASE_FAIL","message":"No database connection: connect() has not been called. ..."}
```
Note vs. the original report: in 0.42.1.0 the **in-cycle `sync` phase** now also fails on this path, not just `synthesize`/minion promotion.

#### Audit trace (matches the diagnosis here)
`~/.gbrain/audit/db-disconnect-*.jsonl` captures the module-singleton teardown from the batch-retry reconnect path:
```json
{"engine_kind":"postgres","connection_style":"module",
 "caller_stack":"at disconnect (src/core/postgres-engine.ts:207:7)\n at async reconnect (src/core/postgres-engine.ts:4658:24)\n at async withRetry (src/core/retry.ts:269:20)\n at async batchRetry (src/core/postgres-engine.ts:1928:20)",
 "command":"dream"}
```
`db.ts` disconnect (now at `db.ts:237` in 0.42.1.0) still carries the comment "*db.ts is always the module-singleton path by construction; no instance-pool callers go through here*" and sets `sql = null`. `reconnect()` rebuilds the instance pool via `this._savedConfig` but leaves the module singleton null, so concurrent/subsequent module-`getConnection()` callers (sync + synthesize) throw. Same mechanism described above; the `batchRetry` reconnect is the trigger we captured.

#### Ruled out (so it's not re-suggested)
- `gbrain init --supabase` / `init --url <same>` — no effect (19 phases connect fine; config is correct).
- Direct → Session-mode pooler — no effect.
- Clearing stale `gbrain_cycle_locks` — unrelated.
- **Standalone `gbrain sync --all` + `gbrain embed --stale` succeed (exit 0)** — isolates the fault to the in-cycle module-singleton path, not sync logic or the DB.

#### Confirming the workaround
The `db.disconnect()` gate posted above (only release the singleton on explicit full shutdown) is consistent with what we see; we can validate it against our Supabase setup if a candidate patch lands. Of the three suggested durable fixes, (a) "don't tear down the shared module singleton inside `reconnect()` — let postgres.js's pool self-heal" matches our trace most directly.

Happy to run a patched build against a ~4,660-page Postgres brain and report cycle results.

**Adjacent gap in the same federated-read-scope class:** the four **takes read ops don't apply source / `federated_read` scope at all**, while page reads and `get_calibration_profile` do.

`takes` has no `source_id` column of its own (`src/core/migrate.ts:1191`) — it's scoped only through `JOIN pages p ON p.id = t.page_id` → `pages.source_id`. But none of the four read ops thread `sourceScopeOpts(ctx)`:

| op | handler | engine read |
|----|---------|-------------|
| `takes_list` | `operations.ts:1701` | `listTakes` (`postgres-engine.ts:4310`) |
| `takes_search` | `operations.ts:1727` | `searchTakes` (`:4343`) |
| `takes_scorecard` | `operations.ts:1754` | `getScorecard` (`:4512`) |
| `takes_calibration` | `operations.ts:1780` | `getCalibrationCurve` (`:4555`) |

The engine SQL never filters on `pages.source_id`; the only filter applied is `takesHoldersAllowList`, which is a *holder* allow-list (orthogonal to source). So on a multi-source brain a `federated_read` client can read a page body across its granted sources via `get_page` (post-sweep), yet the takes on those same pages are unscoped — inconsistent with `get_calibration_profile`, which already routes through `sourceScopeOpts(ctx)` (`operations.ts:3196`; its op description even states "federated_read scopes see the union of allowed sources").

**Fix shape (matching this sweep):** thread `sourceScopeOpts(ctx)` into the four takes handlers and add a `pages.source_id` filter to the engine reads. `listTakes` / `searchTakes` already `JOIN pages`, so it's an extra `AND (<ids> IS NULL OR p.source_id = ANY(<ids>))`; `getScorecard` / `getCalibrationCurve` query `FROM takes` without the join, so they need an `EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM pages p WHERE p.id = takes.page_id AND …)` (or a join). ### Additional symptom: the same uncommitted write-through silently freezes `sync_freshness` and makes the doctor's remediation self-defeating

Hit this independently on a local brain (engine 0.42.53.0; verified against `master`). Beyond the durability/data-loss angle, the uncommitted write-through from #1 produces a confusing **freshness** failure:

- `last_sync_at` is only stamped when `last_commit` advances (`writeSyncAnchor`, `src/commands/sync.ts` — *"last_sync_at bookmarked on every last_commit advance"*, the `now()` write lives only inside the `which === 'last_commit'` branch). Since write-through never commits, HEAD never moves, so `last_sync_at` freezes at the last real commit — even as the dream/enrichment cycle writes new content daily.
- `gbrain doctor`'s `sync_freshness` check then reports `Source 'default' last synced 61h ago … brain search is stale!. Run \`gbrain sync --source <id>\` for each stale source` (`src/commands/doctor.ts:3564` + the fail-branch message at `:3586`).
- **Running that remediation does nothing** — `sync` keys off the commit diff and never imports uncommitted working-tree changes. The user re-runs the suggested command and the alarm persists (observed: re-ran `sync --source default`, `last_sync_at` did not move because there were no new commits to drain; only the one source with genuine new commits advanced).
- The doctor's git short-circuit (`isSourceUnchangedSinceSync(..., { requireCleanWorkingTree: 'ignore-untracked' })` at `doctor.ts:3526-3533`) *correctly* declines to mark these sources fresh, because the tree has modified **tracked** files (`git status --porcelain --untracked-files=no` is non-empty). But the surfaced message points at `sync`, not at the real fix (commit the write-through).

So the same missing commit step manifests three ways: silent data loss (this issue), a frozen freshness stamp, and a doctor recommendation that can't resolve itself. A fix for #1 (commit write-through after enrichment/dream) resolves all three.

Until then, the `sync_freshness` message is arguably misleading in this case — when the only thing standing between HEAD and "fresh" is a dirty **tracked** working tree on a write-through source, it could detect that and recommend a commit (or `gbrain sources harden` once that path actually commits modifications, per #2) instead of a `sync` that is a guaranteed no-op.

Took a close read of this with an eye toward building on it — really glad to see the placeholder retriever finally getting grounded. Two blocking items (one is a compile error), a few non-blocking notes, then a forward-compat note since I'm planning a two-track grading layer on top of this.

## Blocking

**1. `defaultEvidenceRetriever` signature not updated to the widened `EvidenceRetrieverFn`.**
`src/core/cycle/grade-takes.ts:299` — the diff widens `EvidenceRetrieverFn` to `(take, scope, engine) => Promise<string>`, but `defaultEvidenceRetriever` still declares two params `(take, _scope)`. It's exported and used as an `evidenceRetriever` in `test/grade-takes.test.ts`, so this is a TS assignability error. Fix: add the unused third param `_engine: BrainEngine`.

**2. `minAgeMonths` default is incoherent across the two layers.**
`src/core/cycle.ts` passes `minAgeMonths: configNumber('cycle.grade_takes.min_age_months', 0)`, while the phase falls back to `?? 6` when the option is absent. Once cycle.ts supplies the value, the 6-month safety net silently becomes 0 — every brand-new take is immediately eligible on an unconfigured brain, inverting the age-gate intent. Pick one number and make both layers agree (config default `6` to match the phase, or document that `0` = "no minimum" intentionally).

## Non-blocking

**3.** `hybridEvidenceRetriever`'s `since` filter rides the engine's `afterDate`/`effective_date` SQL filter, so on a brain with sparse `effective_date` coverage pages get excluded before `formatGradeEvidenceFromResults` ever sees them — almost always returning "unavailable" with no operator-facing signal explaining why. A line in the function doc calling out that dependency would save a debugging session.

**4.** `evidenceHasCitedSnippets` (`:272`) keys off `^Source:`/`^Snippet:` with `/m`. Correct for the current marker, but if a judge ever echoes those tokens in its reasoning the guard could pass spuriously — worth a forward-compat note.

## Nits

- `test/grade-takes.test.ts` constructs the `UNAVAILABLE_EVIDENCE_MARKER` string inline rather than importing the constant — if the marker text changes the test silently passes against the old string. Import the constant (or expose via `__testing`).
- Consider naming the `insertGradeCache` helper's `applied` param `wasApplied` to avoid colliding with the outer `shouldApply` in readers' heads.

## What's done well

The pre-judge guard fires *after* the idempotency lookup and *before* any gateway call, so a retry never pays twice — exactly the right placement. `insertGradeCache` genuinely de-duplicates the SQL. `normalizeDateOnly` handling `YYYY-MM → YYYY-MM-15` is a thoughtful edge case, and the new `evidence_unavailable` counter gives operators visibility into how often the guard fires.

## Forward-compat (not a blocker)

I'm planning a follow-up two-track layer: per-kind age gates (`min_age_months.bet`/`.take`), grading `kind='take'` opinions as a separate "opinion track record" (hit-rate, not Brier), alongside the bet Brier track. This PR's design makes that clean — `hybridEvidenceRetriever` is a proper named export satisfying the `EvidenceRetrieverFn` seam, and `{KIND}` is already threaded into the judge prompt so the scorecard can read it from existing cache rows with no schema change. The one thing worth fixing here first is finding #2 (the `minAgeMonths` incoherence), since the follow-up splits that single scalar into two keys — better to settle the number once than migrate the confusion into two config paths.

Read this closely since it's the promotion path a lot depends on (#2411/#2269) — the core `acceptTakeProposal` logic is tight and the review-first principle is enforced throughout. Two blocking items, a few non-blocking notes, and a forward-compat note for a grading layer I'm planning on top.

## Blocking

**1. `pg_advisory_xact_lock` will throw on PGLite, rolling back the accept transaction.**
`src/core/take-proposals.ts` — the inner transaction calls `SELECT pg_advisory_xact_lock($1::bigint)` bare. PGLite doesn't implement it and throws, unwinding `engine.transaction`, so `takes propose accept` hard-fails on any PGLite install. The codebase already wraps advisory locks defensively (`operations.ts:1148-1152`); same fix here:
```ts
try {
  await tx.executeRaw('SELECT pg_advisory_xact_lock($1::bigint)', [pageId]);
} catch { /* PGLite single-process; no cross-process race to guard */ }
```

**2. An `accepted` proposal with `promoted_row_num = null` falls through to a confusing throw.**
The idempotency fast-path is `status === 'accepted' && promoted_row_num !== null`. If a prior accept partially committed (UPDATE landed, RETURNING didn't), the row is `accepted` with a null row_num and the next call hits `if (status !== 'pending') throw` — an opaque error instead of surfacing the partial state. Either early-return on `status === 'accepted'` (with a warning), or add a NOT NULL constraint so the half-state can't exist.

## Non-blocking

**3.** `rejectTakeProposal` accepts a `reason`, returns it, but never persists it (no `rejection_reason` column). The op description is transparent about this, which is good — but a schema migration to persist it (or a `migrate.ts` TODO) would keep it from reading like silent data loss to a future contributor.

**4.** `rejectTakeProposal` only blocks on `accepted`, so it will silently stamp a `superseded` proposal as `rejected`. If superseded→reject is valid re-triage, document it; otherwise guard it. No test covers the `superseded` path.

**5.** The markdown `existsSync(path)` check runs before `engine.transaction` (minor TOCTOU). Fine for current usage; worth noting for a hardened remote path.

## Nits

- CLI `since=(unset: no real claim-date)` is verbose for the terminal — `since=<none>` reads cleaner.
- A test asserting `takes_propose_list.scope === 'read'` and that the write ops require `proposal_id` would explicitly close the "wrong scope exposed over MCP" scenario.

## What's done well

`acceptTakeProposal` is careful: re-fetches the proposal *for update* inside the transaction, dedups against active takes by lowercased claim, writes markdown before the DB mirror, and rolls back the filesystem write on exception. The `since_date` fallback-suppression (dropping `source='fallback'` dates) is a good data-quality call. MCP ops are correctly `read`/`write`-scoped, the remote-trust model follows the established `ctx.sourceId` pattern, and `FakeProposalEngine` is thorough enough to catch real promotion bugs without a live DB.

## Forward-compat (not a blocker)

For a two-track grader on top of this, a promoted take needs `kind`, `weight`, `since_date`, and a path back to the proposal — all four survive (`kind`/`holder`/`weight` carried verbatim, `since_date` resolved with fallback-suppression, `source` stamped `proposal:${id}`). One thing to surface for the follow-up rather than block here: `kind` is carried from the proposal with no override at accept time. Since all current proposals are `kind='take'`, minting a gradeable `kind='bet'` will need either a kind override at accept (`--as bet`) or a post-accept update — neither exists today. That's the natural seam where "elect this opinion into a bet" would live.

Great survey — but I want to push on the "Suggested direction." A pluggable **text** extractor, even the best one (marker, markitdown), solves the wrong problem for the corpus you opened with (a `_literature/` vault of papers). Every option except vendor-LLM converts the page to a linear string — which is exactly where a table's cells and a figure's content are lost. `pdftotext` turning `55.2/66.1` into `55.266.1` isn't a quality bug a better extractor fixes; it's what happens when text is the representation at all.

So the interface question isn't "which `PDFExtractor`" — it's whether the primitive should be a text chunk or a **visual semantic unit** (a table/figure region, multimodally embedded, read by vision on demand). For prose PDFs the extractor path is fine; for research papers it structurally can't get there. And the high-fidelity path can still satisfy your open question #2 — it's **Bun-pure** (`pdftoppm` + the gateway, no Python bridge). Full argument + a working implementation in #2543.

Also reproduces on **`anthropic:claude-sonnet-4-6`** with parallel tool calls — the "move subagent jobs to Anthropic" workaround in the OP is not sufficient.

**Env**: gbrain 0.42.56.0 (`6461790`), Postgres engine, `agent.use_gateway_loop=true`, `models.dream.synthesize=anthropic:claude-sonnet-4-6`, worker `jobs work --queue default` (concurrency 1).

Root cause found + local workaround verified.

**Root cause:** the subagent gateway loop pushes tool results as **v1 Anthropic-shape blocks** (`{type: 'tool_result', tool_use_id, content, is_error}` — `src/core/minions/handlers/subagent.ts` ~L601-702), but `toModelMessages()` in `src/core/ai/gateway.ts` only matches the v2 hyphen shape (`b.type === 'tool-result'` with `toolCallId`). The v1 blocks fall through to the generic branch, so the wire request reaches the OpenAI-compatible provider with assistant `tool_calls` but **no `role:"tool"` messages at all** — the provider rejects with "Tool results are missing for tool calls ...". The Anthropic SDK accepts v1 blocks natively, which is why the Anthropic loop never surfaces this.

**Verified fix (local patch):** normalize both shapes inside `toModelMessages` — match `b.type === 'tool-result' || b.type === 'tool_result'`, then `toolCallId = b.toolCallId ?? b.tool_use_id`, `output = b.output ?? b.content`, `isError = b.isError ?? b.is_error`. After the patch the wire skeleton is healthy (`assistant(tool_calls: [call_6c42…])` followed by `role:"tool", tool_call_id: call_6c42…`) and the same previously-failing transcript synthesizes to completion.
